newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian labour talks stumble, attention on budget.
newsitem.headline: Italian labour talks stumble, attention on budget.

text.p: The Italian government has postponed a national conference on unemployment originally scheduled for later this week after failing to strike an agreement with unions and employers on new labour contracts.
The delay gives Prime Minister Romano Prodi's centre-left administration more time to work on the problematic 1997 budget which is expected to be presented on Friday.

Treasury Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi wants to introduce as tough a package as possible, including cutbacks to health and pensions spending, to prepare Italy for the launch of the single European currency in 1999.

But a key government supporter, the hard left Communist Refoundation, has refused to sanction any move on sensitive welfare spending and has called for an urgent meeting with Prodi and his parliamentary allies on Monday.
Faced by a dense week of budget meetings, Prodi decided to put back the long-awaited unemployment conference in Naples until an unspecified date next month.
By then, he hopes he can go to the forum with an accord on new working practices aimed at easing Italy's high jobless total which is stuck at just over 12 percent of the workforce.

Talks between the government, unions and business leaders on ways to cut Italy's army of unemployed stumbled on Saturday when employers' federation Confindustria objected to plans to reduce the length of the working week from 48 hours to 40.
The change has to be introduced by the end of the year under a European Union directive, but Confindustria is worried that the new limit will lead to a leap in overtime payments.
Despite the unexpected delay, all sides are confident an agreement will be found when they meet again on Tuesday.

"We are very close to reaching a deal," Labour Minister Tiziano Treu was quoted as saying in newspapers on Sunday. "We thought it wise to put off the employment conference because the coming week will be very busy...what with the budget," he added.

The government has already said the package will seek to reduce Italy's annual budget deficit by 32.4 trillion lire ($21.2 billion) next year, but analysts are sceptical that this target can be hit without action on the generous welfare state.

Ciampi was widely reported to be keen to cut two trillion lire off pensions spending, but Fausto Bertinotti, leader of the Communist Refoundation party, warned on Saturday that Italy's government could fall if it touched the benefits.
"We ask the government to quickly eliminate the threat (of pension cuts), which is a threat not only to pensioners but to the government itself," Bertinotti told reporters.
The government controls the upper house of parliament (Senate), but relies on the support of the Refoundation to control the lower house of parliament.
Ciampi's drive for a tougher budget is linked to the planned creation of a single European currency in 1999.

At present Italy fails to meet any of the criteria established by the Maastricht Treaty for countries wishing to sign up for the Euro and a weak budget would put the country even further behind in its bid to meet the Maastricht terms.
Prodi warned in a newspaper interview at the weekend that any delay in joining the Euro could prove fatal.

"I used to think a second group of countries could take part (in monetary union) in a successive phase," Prodi told La Stampa daily. "But I no longer believe that...The countries that will be left out (of the first phase of monetary union) will remain only farther and farther behind," he added.
